notes.title: Start here: seven flows through a scheduling platform
notes.body:
cal.diy is a large open-source scheduling platform (a Cal.com codebase): a Next.js web app plus many packages under `cal.diy/packages/`. The study track is `cal.diy/fabledocs/upskill/`.

This quest uses two pages:

1. `01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`: seven traced flows (create a booking, fetch slots, reserve a slot, cancel, render the booking page, deliver webhooks, update an event type). Each has a step table with file and line anchors.
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`: what runs after a booking is written.

The repository is big; do not try to read it all. For each flow, open only the files in its table, at the cited lines, and read a little above and below. Many quiz questions hinge on one condition in one function (a status value, an operator, an environment fallback), so read conditions character by character. Short file names in the tables such as `util.ts` are ambiguous in a monorepo; use the full paths given at the top of each flow.

notes.title: Concept: idempotency keys, short caches and slot holds
notes.body:
**Idempotency at the database.** `packages/prisma/extensions/booking-idempotency-key.ts` is a Prisma client extension: it intercepts `booking.create` and `booking.update` before the query runs. Read both hooks and note the exact condition under which each one touches `idempotencyKey`, and what the key is built from. Think about what a unique key built from those inputs prevents.

**A two-second cache.** `withSlotsCache` in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots/util.ts` wraps slot computation in Redis. Read how the cache key is built, how the TTL is computed from the environment, and what happens on each kind of Redis failure. Look up how `JSON.stringify` orders object properties and how `parseInt` handles non-numeric strings.

**Slot holds.** `reserveSlot.handler.ts` writes `SelectedSlots` rows so two bookers do not grab the same time. List each condition that must be true for the write to happen, and what the handler does after the write block regardless.

excerpts.quote: `findReservedByOthers` — is someone else holding this slot?

readMore.why: The whole idempotency extension; under 60 lines.

notes.title: Concept: who may cancel, and who may edit
notes.body:
**Cancelling.** `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts` is a sequence of guards before any side effect. Number them in order and write the status code and message of each. Pay attention to how `isCancellationUserHost` is computed: which inputs come from the server and which come from the request body. Then read `isCancellationReasonRequired` in `cancellationReason.ts` and note what a missing setting falls back to.

**Editing event types.** `eventOwnerProcedure` in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/util.ts` splits personal events from team events. Read the team branch and follow the `PermissionCheckService` it uses to its definition.

**Webhooks and anonymous callers.** In `sendPayload.ts`, read `createWebhookSignature` and the fetch options. In `apps/web/pages/api/book/event.ts`, note what the route passes as the user id when there is no session.

excerpts.quote: cancellation is where *authorization* actually lives (unlike creation)

readMore.why: The side-effects chapter: tasks, retries and webhook delivery.

notes.title: Why a pending booking gets no idempotency key
notes.body:
The create hook generates a key only inside `if (args.data.status === BookingStatus.ACCEPTED)`. A booking created as PENDING (it needs host confirmation) passes through to `query(args)` with no key, so the unique constraint does not deduplicate unconfirmed bookings.

- *uuidv5 from start, end and user id*: that is the key for ACCEPTED creates only.
- *Random uuidv4*: the extension never generates random keys.
- *Rejects the create*: the hook never throws; it only adds a field.

notes.title: Why cancelling clears the idempotency key
notes.body:
The update hook sets `args.data.idempotencyKey = null` when the new status is CANCELLED or REJECTED. The key is a uuidv5 of start time, end time and user id, so leaving it in place would block any new ACCEPTED booking for the same slot and user with a unique-constraint error. Nulling it frees the slot.

- *Kept forever*: the hook explicitly nulls it.
- *Replaced with a new key*: no new key is generated on update.
- *Only acts on create*: the extension has update and updateMany hooks too.

notes.title: Why an invalid SLOTS_CACHE_TTL means 2000 ms
notes.body:
The TTL is `parseInt(process.env.SLOTS_CACHE_TTL ?? "", 10) || DEFAULT_SLOTS_CACHE_TTL`. `parseInt("abc", 10)` is NaN, NaN is falsy, so the `||` picks the default of 2000 ms. The result is then stored with `redisClient.set` without awaiting it.

- *0 ms*: 0 would also be falsy and fall back to 2000; it is never used as a TTL.
- *Throws*: parseInt does not throw on bad input.
- *Passed to Redis*: the value given to Redis is the number from this expression.

notes.title: Why property order splits the cache
notes.body:
`withSlotsCache` uses `JSON.stringify(args.input)` as the Redis key. `JSON.stringify` writes properties in the object's insertion order and does not sort them, so two equal inputs built in different orders produce two different strings and two cache entries. The guide lists this as the key-stability risk. Requests through the tRPC getSchedule route are less exposed, because the Zod object schema rebuilds the input in schema key order before the handler sees it.

- *Sorted alphabetically*: JSON.stringify does not sort.
- *Hash of sorted values*: there is no hashing or sorting step.
- *Random nonce*: nothing random goes into the key.

notes.title: Why the first seat of a seated event is not held
notes.body:
For an event type with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, the handler looks for an ACCEPTED booking at that slot. With no booking yet it sets `shouldReserveSlot = false` (the comment: "If there is no booking yet then don't reserve the slot"). The upsert block is skipped, but the cookie code after it still runs and the handler returns the uid.

- *One seat reserved*: for a seated event, a hold is written only when an existing booking still has seats left.
- *NOT_FOUND*: that error is for a missing event type or a failed upsert.
- *Every seat reserved*: nothing is written at all.

excerpts.quote: If there is no booking yet then don't reserve the slot

notes.title: Why a dry run writes nothing
notes.body:
The write block runs only when `eventType && shouldReserveSlot && !reservedBySomeoneElse && !_isDryRun`. With `_isDryRun` true the `selectedSlots.upsert` calls never happen. The handler still reads existing reservations and still sets the uid cookie.

- *Row with releaseAt now*: no row is written.
- *Row flagged as dry run*: there is no such flag.
- *PENDING booking*: reserveSlot never creates bookings.

notes.title: Why a second cancel is refused
notes.body:
The first guard after loading the booking is `if (bookingToDelete.status === BookingStatus.CANCELLED)`, which throws HttpError 400 "This booking has already been cancelled." The comment explains the reason: a reschedule marks the old booking CANCELLED while keeping its calendar event, and a later cancel must not delete that event.

- *Success again*: the handler throws instead.
- *Deletes the calendar event again*: preventing that is the point of the guard.
- *404*: the booking is loaded; the status check rejects it.

excerpts.quote: message: "This booking has already been cancelled.",

notes.title: Why an attendee may cancel without a reason by default
notes.body:
`isCancellationReasonRequired(setting, isHost)` uses `setting ?? MANDATORY_HOST_ONLY`. For that requirement it returns `isHost`. The attendee is not the host (no matching user id or email), so no reason is required, the reason guard passes and cancellation continues to the next checks.

- *Always required*: that is MANDATORY_BOTH, which is not the default.
- *401, hosts only*: attendees may cancel; 401 is only for seated events without a seat reference.
- *Host approval*: there is no approval step in cancellation.

notes.title: Why cancelledBy can make a caller count as host
notes.body:
`isCancellationUserHost` is `bookingToDelete.userId === userId || bookingToDelete.user.email === cancelledBy`. `cancelledBy` comes from the request body, so an anonymous caller who sends the host's email is treated as the host. Under MANDATORY_HOST_ONLY a reason is then required, and the missing reason throws HttpError 400 "Cancellation reason is required". The guide flags the email-based host match.

- *Attendee, goes through*: the email match makes isHost true.
- *401 unauthenticated*: the function does not require a session.
- *Skips remaining checks*: being treated as host does not bypass the other guards.

notes.title: Who may cancel a seated booking
notes.body:
For an event type with `seatsPerTimeSlot` and no `seatReferenceUid` in the request, the handler checks whether the caller is one of the event type's hosts or its owner. If neither, it throws HttpError with statusCode 401 and "User not a host of this event". Attendees cancel their own seat by sending its seatReferenceUid.

- *Own seat cancelled*: without a seat reference the handler cannot tell which seat.
- *Whole booking cancelled*: the guard stops the request first.
- *403*: the code uses 401 here.

notes.title: Why the team permission check always passes
notes.body:
`eventTypes/util.ts` declares a local `class PermissionCheckService` whose `checkPermission` simply returns true. The team branch of `eventOwnerProcedure` calls that local class, so `hasPermission` is always true and the FORBIDDEN throw never runs, whoever the caller is. Personal events are still checked properly. The guide calls this the authorization boundary you can break.

- *false, FORBIDDEN*: the stub never returns false.
- *Throws, PBAC not configured*: the stub has no configuration to fail on.
- *false except delete*: the same stub answers every permission string.

notes.title: What a secretless webhook is signed with
notes.body:
`createWebhookSignature` returns an HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the body when a secret exists, and the literal string "no-secret-provided" otherwise. `_sendPayload` always sends the header, so a receiver that only checks for its presence would accept unsigned deliveries; receivers must reject that value.

- *HMAC with an empty key*: the secret branch is skipped entirely.
- *No header*: the header is always set.
- *Plain SHA-256 of the body*: no unkeyed hash is computed.

notes.title: How an anonymous booking is identified
notes.body:
`POST /api/book/event` calls `getServerSession({ req })`, which yields no user for a visitor who is not signed in. The route passes `userId: session?.user?.id || -1` in `bookingMeta`, so anonymous bookings carry -1. Anonymous booking is expected: the booker is usually not a user of the platform.

- *null*: the || fallback gives -1, not null.
- *0, system user*: no system user is involved.
- *401*: the route does not require a session.
